parsed_answer.content:
When designing high-performance data pipelines or algorithms in Java that require FIFO queue or LIFO stack semantics, developers frequently debate between ArrayDeque and LinkedList. While both implement the Deque interface, their underlying memory layout and performance characteristics diverge significantly. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list where every element is wrapped in a discrete Node object containing pointers to its predecessor and successor. This architecture incurs heavy heap fragmentation, high memory overhead due to object headers and reference pointers (typically 24 bytes per node on 64-bit JVMs with compressed OOPs), and poor cache locality because nodes are scattered arbitrarily across the heap.

Conversely, ArrayDeque implements a resizable circular array. It stores elements in a contiguous memory block (an object array), minimizing pointer overhead and capitalizing heavily on CPU cache lines and prefetching mechanisms. As elements are added and removed from both ends, head and tail pointers wrap around the array indices. When capacity is exhausted, the internal array is doubled in size via a swift System.arraycopy operation. Understanding this fundamental trade-off between contiguous allocation and pointer-chaining is critical for writing low-latency Java applications that avoid unnecessary garbage collection pressure.

rows: Bloated (Node object per element with 2 extra pointers)
Low (pointer chasing across disparate heap locations)
Minimal (no node allocation churn during operations)
High (frequent allocation and collection of short-lived Node instances)

items: ArrayDeque doubles its underlying array capacity when it fills up, utilizing bitwise operations (e.g., (elements.length - 1) & (head - 1)) for extremely fast circular index wrapping without heavy modulo division.
LinkedList implements both List and Deque, making it structurally heavier. Each mutation operation allocates a new Node object, directly increasing minor GC frequency under high-throughput workloads.

Stack operations (push/pop) and Queue operations (offer/poll) run in O(1) amortized time for ArrayDeque and strict O(1) worst-case time for LinkedList, though ArrayDeque outperforms LinkedList empirically by orders of magnitude due to hardware-level CPU caching.

parsed_answer.content: Never use LinkedList as a stack or queue in production systems unless you explicitly need O(1) node-removal stability during traversal or need to store null values. In almost all modern enterprise use cases, ArrayDeque serves as the drop-in replacement that yields superior throughput, zero structural node overhead, and vastly reduced GC pauses.
